input.dataset_info: genomic DNA sequences around putative transcriptional pause sites

feature.name: pause_to_plus1_purine_to_pyrimidine
feature.description: Create a binary feature from the 101-nt raw_sequence using 0-based indexing. Let position 50 be the pause site and position 51 be the first downstream nucleotide. Set the feature to 1 if raw_sequence[50] is a purine (A or G) AND raw_sequence[51] is a pyrimidine (C or T). Otherwise set it to 0. In set notation: feature = 1 if raw_sequence[50] in {A,G} and raw_sequence[51] in {C,T}, else 0.
feature.rationale: The strongest features in the population share two simple ideas: (1) the most predictive signal is extremely local to the pause site, especially positions 50 and 51, and (2) simple categorical summaries of the nucleotide work well, such as exact base identity or purine/pyrimidine class. The best feature is position 50 being G, and another strong feature is whether position 51 is a purine, which suggests that the pause-site dinucleotide environment is important. To stay close to these successful ideas but avoid redundancy with any single-base feature, I use the transition between the site base and the immediately downstream base rather than either position alone. A particularly interpretable transition is whether the sequence goes from a purine at the pause site to a pyrimidine at +1. This captures a simple local sequence step that may reflect active-site and next-template-base effects on translocation and nucleotide addition, both relevant to RNA polymerase pausing. It is still easy to explain biologically and computationally, but is not just a repeat of pos_50_is_G or pos_51_is_A/purine.

feature.name: upstream_minus26_to_minus17_GC_rich
feature.description: Create a binary feature from raw_sequence using 0-based indexing. Examine positions 24 through 33 inclusive (10 nt). Count how many nucleotides in this window are G or C. Set the feature to 1 if at least 7 of the 10 positions are G or C; otherwise set it to 0. Formally: feature = 1 if |{i in [24,33] : raw_sequence[i] in {'G','C'}}| >= 7, else 0.
feature.rationale: I first avoided the sequence ideas that are already represented at this node. The path from the root already uses the exact 50-51 dinucleotide class, and the candidate population is heavily concentrated on single-base tests at positions 49/50/51, AT richness immediately upstream (-13 to -1), and GC richness immediately downstream (+1 to +12). To be complementary, I looked for a simple signal in a different region and tied to a different biological mechanism. A well-known contributor to bacterial transcriptional pausing is formation of a nascent RNA pause hairpin, whose stem is often supported by a GC-rich segment roughly 10-20 nt upstream of the active site. Rather than use a complex stem-loop predictor, a simple and interpretable proxy is to test whether a short upstream window in that hairpin-prone region is enriched for G/C. I chose positions 24 through 33 (about -26 to -17 relative to the pause site), which is farther upstream than the existing GC-rich feature at 30-39 and outside the windows already dominated by upstream AT-rich or downstream GC-rich candidates. This makes the feature mechanistically relevant, easy for a biologist to interpret, and less redundant with the current feature set.

feature.name: upstream_minus10_to_minus1_gc_count
feature.description: Using the 101-nt raw_sequence with 0-based indexing, examine the 10 nucleotides immediately upstream of the pause site: positions 40 through 49 inclusive. Count how many of these positions contain G or C. Return this integer count, which ranges from 0 to 10. In set notation: feature = |{i in [40,49] : raw_sequence[i] in {G,C}}|.
feature.rationale: The top-performing candidate features point to two recurring ideas: (1) local sequence determinants very close to the pause site are most useful, and (2) simple, biologically interpretable properties outperform complex combinations. The strongest repeated feature is high GC content in the 10 nt immediately upstream of the pause site, suggesting that upstream GC richness is a consistent signal of pausing, likely because GC-rich RNA:DNA hybrid / nearby duplex sequence can stabilize the elongation complex and slow translocation. There are also good single-position features at the pause site itself, but the current node already conditions on the pause-site/+1 pattern being purine at position 50 and pyrimidine at 51, so using position 50 again would be redundant. To stay complementary to the existing split while preserving the successful theme from the population, I keep the same biological idea but simplify it further to a continuous count rather than a thresholded binary call. This preserves interpretability, avoids committing to a possibly overfit cutoff of 7, and gives the tree flexibility to choose the best threshold at this node.

feature.name: pos_51_is_T
feature.description: Check if position 51 in raw sequence is T
feature.rationale: Basic sequence composition feature checking for T at position 51
feature.code:
def pos_51_is_T(X):
    return X['raw_sequence'].apply(lambda x: x[51] == 'T')

feature.description: Check if position 49 in raw sequence is G
feature.rationale: Basic sequence composition feature checking for G at position 49
feature.code:
def pos_49_is_G(X):
    return X['raw_sequence'].apply(lambda x: x[49] == 'G')

feature.name: pause_site_is_G
feature.description: Create a binary feature from the 101-nt raw_sequence using 0-based indexing, where position 50 is the pause site. Set the feature to 1 if raw_sequence[50] is G. Set it to 0 if raw_sequence[50] is A, C, or T. Because this node already satisfies raw_sequence[50] in {A,G}, this feature effectively distinguishes G from A at the pause site within the current subset.
feature.rationale: The current node already isolates sequences with a purine at the pause site followed by a pyrimidine at +1, and with low GC in the -10 to -1 region. A nonredundant and biologically intuitive next discriminator is the identity of the pause-site nucleotide itself. In many transcription pause contexts, guanine at the RNA 3' end can stabilize the elongation complex differently from adenine because G:C pairing is stronger than A:T pairing in the DNA template context. Thus, among sequences already enriched for purine-to-pyrimidine pause junctions, separating G from A at the exact pause site may capture a clear mechanistic effect on pausing propensity.

feature.name: upstream_minus25_to_minus16_AT_count
feature.description: Create an integer feature from the 101-nt raw_sequence using 0-based indexing. Let position 50 be the pause site. Examine positions 25 through 34 inclusive (upstream positions -25 to -16). Count how many of these 10 nucleotides are A or T. Return this count, ranging from 0 to 10. In set notation: feature = |{i in [25,34] : raw_sequence[i] in {A,T}}|.
feature.rationale: The current path already fixes a purine at the pause site followed by a pyrimidine at +1, and it also requires GC richness immediately upstream at positions 40-49. The existing candidate features mostly explore three nearby ideas: more GC content downstream, pause-site identity, or upstream T runs very close to the site. To avoid redundancy, I chose a different and simple mechanism: an A/T-rich tract farther upstream, in the region that could correspond to the upstream half of a pause hairpin stem/loop context or generally lower nucleic-acid stability behind the polymerase. This is biologically relevant because lower GC and higher AT in the more distal upstream region can reduce duplex stability and create a sequence environment distinct from the already-selected GC-rich immediate upstream segment. It is also complementary to the current node because it probes a non-overlapping window (positions 25-34) and asks about upstream instability rather than the already-used immediate upstream GC enrichment or the repeatedly tested T-run and downstream composition features.

feature.name: central_minus3_to_plus1_GC_rich
feature.description: Create a binary feature from the 101-nt raw_sequence using 0-based indexing, where position 50 is the pause site. Examine positions 47 through 51 inclusive (corresponding to -3 to +1 relative to the pause site). Count the number of nucleotides in this 5-nt window that are G or C. Set the feature to 1 if at least 4 of the 5 positions are G or C; otherwise set it to 0. Formally: feature = 1 if |{i in [47,51] : raw_sequence[i] in {'G','C'}}| >= 4, else 0.
feature.rationale:
I first identified the common pattern among the best candidate features. The top-scoring population is dominated by very local sequence context around the pause site, especially short GC-rich windows spanning roughly -3 to +2. Several strong features are variants of the same idea: proximal GC enrichment near the active center is informative, likely because GC-rich nucleic acids are more thermodynamically stable and can disfavor forward translocation, which is relevant to RNA polymerase pausing.

Next I checked the existing path conditions to avoid redundancy. The current node has already used: (1) the nucleotide class relationship between the pause site and +1, (2) a distal upstream GC-rich window from -26 to -17, and (3) the specific identity of +1 being T. So I should avoid another feature that mainly re-tests position +1 alone or the distal upstream region.

Given the common high-performing idea, the simplest complementary feature is a short GC-content summary centered on the pause site but shifted slightly upstream so it captures the immediate active-center neighborhood without depending too heavily on +1 identity. This keeps the feature biologically interpretable and less redundant with the previous splits. A GC-rich central window is intuitive for biologists as a proxy for local duplex/RNA-DNA hybrid stability that can promote pausing.

feature.name: upstream_minus10_to_minus1_AT_fraction
feature.description: Create a numeric feature from the 101-nt raw_sequence using 0-based indexing. Consider the 10-nt window immediately upstream of the pause site: positions 40 through 49 inclusive (corresponding to -10 through -1 relative to the pause site at position 50). Count the number of nucleotides in this window that are A or T. Define the feature as this count divided by 10. Formally: feature = (1/10) * |{i in [40,49] : raw_sequence[i] in {'A','T'}}|. The feature ranges from 0.0 to 1.0.
feature.rationale: To propose a useful split, I first avoided features that are redundant with the current path: +1 is already fixed as T, the node already excludes a purine-to-pyrimidine pause/+1 transition, and it already excludes a GC-rich upstream window from positions 24 to 33. I also avoided repeating the existing candidate population, which is dominated by single-nucleotide checks near the pause site (positions 32, 41, 44, 48, 49, 50, 79). To explore a different and still interpretable mechanism, I focused on the immediate upstream DNA tract from -10 to -1 (positions 40 to 49), which can influence local DNA flexibility and the stability of the transcription complex. In particular, A/T-rich DNA is generally easier to melt and more flexible than G/C-rich DNA, which could affect pausing without reusing the exact pause-site nucleotide or the excluded upstream GC-rich window. A simple summary of this mechanism is the A/T fraction in the last 10 nt before the pause site. This is biologically intuitive, computationally clear, and complementary to the prior features because it captures local upstream composition rather than a single base or the already-used -26 to -17 region.

feature.name: plus1_is_GC
feature.description: Create a binary feature from the 101-nt raw_sequence using 0-based indexing. Let position 51 be the first downstream nucleotide (+1 relative to the pause site at position 50). Set the feature to 1 if raw_sequence[51] is G or C; otherwise set it to 0. In set notation: feature = 1 if raw_sequence[51] in {'G','C'}, else 0.
feature.rationale: The existing path already conditions on three ideas: (1) the pause-site to +1 dinucleotide is not a purine-to-pyrimidine step, (2) there is a GC-rich tract farther upstream (-26 to -17), and (3) the base immediately upstream at -1 is not G. So a useful new feature should stay near the pause center but avoid reusing those exact positions/patterns. The only population feature tests whether the pause-site base itself is a pyrimidine; that suggests the top idea is that local nucleotide identity at the active center matters. A simple and complementary refinement is to look one base downstream, at +1, because downstream DNA identity can affect translocation and initial post-pause elongation, yet it is not fixed by the current node: the node only excludes one specific class where site is purine and +1 is pyrimidine. Within the remaining sequences, whether +1 is specifically G/C versus A/T can still separate classes. This is biologically interpretable because a G/C immediately downstream can increase local duplex stability and may influence RNA polymerase translocation/pause escape. It is also computationally simple and nonredundant with the current splits.

feature.name: downstream_plus2_to_plus6_T_count
feature.description: Using the 101-nt raw_sequence with 0-based indexing, let position 50 be the pause site. Examine the five nucleotides at positions 52 through 56 inclusive (corresponding to downstream positions +2 through +6). Count how many of these positions are T. Return this integer count, ranging from 0 to 5. In set notation: feature = |{i in [52,56] : raw_sequence[i] = T}|.
feature.rationale: The current node already fixes three aspects of the local pause signal: the pause-site base is G, the +1 base is a pyrimidine, and the -10 to -1 region is AT-rich overall. The existing candidate feature also focuses on a single upstream position (-1 = position 49), so using that again would be redundant. To explore a different and still simple mechanism, I moved to the downstream side of the pause, which is not constrained except for +1 being C/T. A biologically interpretable signal there is whether the DNA just downstream is T-rich, because A/T-rich downstream sequence is easier to melt and can affect the stability of the transcription bubble and immediate post-pause translocation state. To keep the feature simple and non-overfit, I use a very short window immediately downstream (+2 to +6), avoiding the already constrained +1 position and avoiding complex motif definitions. This gives a compact, intuitive feature that is distinct from both the root-to-node conditions and the initial population.

feature.name: upstream_minus11_to_minus2_G_enriched
feature.description: Using 0-based indexing on raw_sequence, examine positions 39 through 48 inclusive (10 nt, corresponding to -11 to -2 relative to the pause site at position 50). Count how many nucleotides in this window are G. Set the feature to 1 if at least 4 of these 10 positions are G; otherwise set it to 0. Formally: feature = 1 if |{i in [39,48] : raw_sequence[i] == 'G'}| >= 4, else 0.
feature.rationale: The best-scoring candidate features repeatedly point to two localized signals: (1) strong single-base effects in the immediate downstream region, especially at positions 51 and 53, and (2) G enrichment in the upstream/near-site region, especially around positions 39-49. Because the current path already used position 51, a central GC-rich window (47-51), and an upstream GC-rich window at 24-33, a good complementary feature should capture the same broad idea of local sequence control of pausing but in a nearby, not-yet-used window. A simple way to do this is to summarize the upstream G enrichment suggested by several top features (positions 39, 42, 43, 46, 49) without using multiple separate indicators. This remains biologically interpretable because a G-rich segment just upstream of the pause site can contribute to a more stable transcription bubble/RNA-DNA hybrid context and may influence RNA polymerase translocation and pausing. I therefore chose a compact binary feature measuring whether the immediate upstream segment from -11 to -2 is G-rich, which captures the common signal from the top features while avoiding redundancy with the already-used 24-33 and 47-51 windows.

feature.name: minus1_and_pause_site_GC_count
feature.description: Create a numeric feature from raw_sequence using 0-based indexing. Let position 50 be the pause site and position 49 be the nucleotide immediately upstream (-1). Count how many of these two positions are G or C. The feature value is therefore 0, 1, or 2. Formally: feature = 1{raw_sequence[49] in {'G','C'}} + 1{raw_sequence[50] in {'G','C'}}.
feature.rationale: I aimed for a feature that is biologically meaningful for pausing but clearly different from both the current path and the existing candidate features. The current node already uses: +1 is T, the pause/+1 step is not purine→pyrimidine, the immediate upstream 10-nt region is broadly A/T-rich, and a more distal upstream region is not GC-rich. The candidate population further explores nearby single-base identities, short downstream composition windows, a local inverted repeat, and A/T runs immediately upstream. To avoid redundancy, I moved to a different simple mechanism: the strength of the base pair exactly at the pause site and its immediate upstream neighbor, summarized as the count of G/C nucleotides at positions -1 and 0. Biologically, these two positions sit at the upstream edge of the active-center region / RNA-DNA hybrid boundary and can influence local duplex stability and the energetics of forward translocation. A GC pair is stronger than an AT pair, so a GC-enriched dinucleotide here is an intuitive proxy for a more stable local core around the paused complex. This is complementary because it does not reuse the broad upstream A/T fraction, the distal upstream GC-richness, the fixed +1 T, or a single exact identity at position 50 or 49 alone. It is also distinct from the candidate set because it captures local pair strength over a 2-nt core window rather than composition in the same windows already tested or another single-position check.

feature.name: downstream_plus20_to_plus30_gc_count
feature.description: Using the 101-nt raw_sequence with 0-based indexing and pause site at position 50, examine positions 70 through 80 inclusive (downstream positions +20 to +30). Count how many of these 11 nucleotides are G or C. Return this integer count, ranging from 0 to 11. In set notation: feature = |{i in [70,80] : raw_sequence[i] in {G,C}}|.
feature.rationale: I avoided proposing another feature that repeats the path’s existing signals: the node already conditions on a purine-to-pyrimidine step at positions 50->51, strong GC enrichment in the immediate upstream region (40 to 49), lower A/T farther upstream (25 to 34), and specifically that position 48 is not T. I also avoided the current feature population’s main themes, which are dominated by more nearby upstream GC measurements, pause-site G identity, and immediate downstream A/T or T-rich windows. To explore a genuinely different and still biologically intuitive mechanism, I shifted farther downstream to sequence that, once transcribed, could form part of a nascent RNA hairpin stem. A simple proxy for this is GC richness in a short window around +20 to +30, because GC-rich RNA segments are more capable of forming stable stem structures, and pause stabilization is often associated with nascent RNA secondary structure forming upstream of the polymerase. This is complementary to the already used upstream-hybrid and immediate +1/+2 local composition features, and it is simpler and less redundant than modeling a full hairpin.

feature.name: upstream_minus8_to_minus1_T_count
feature.description: Using the 101-nt raw_sequence with 0-based indexing, let position 50 be the pause site. Examine the 8 nucleotides immediately upstream of the pause site, positions 42 through 49 inclusive (corresponding to -8 through -1). Count how many of these positions are T. Return this integer count, ranging from 0 to 8. In set notation: feature = |{i in [42,49] : raw_sequence[i] = 'T'}|.
feature.rationale: I first excluded feature ideas that would be redundant with the path to the current node. The node already fixes the central dinucleotide class (position 50 is a purine and position 51 is not C, together with the earlier split meaning +1 is a pyrimidine, effectively T here), and it already uses two upstream composition summaries: GC-richness in -10..-1 and AT-richness in -25..-16. I also avoided the main directions already explored in the candidate population, which are mostly downstream +2 windows based on A/T or T counts, plus a single-base feature at -1 and one isolated upstream position. To explore a clearly different but still simple biological mechanism, I focused on the tract immediately upstream of the pause site as a potential U-rich nascent RNA segment. In the DNA coding strand representation given here, T bases in positions -8 to -1 correspond to U-rich RNA just before the active center, which is biologically relevant because a U-rich RNA:DNA hybrid is weaker and is classically associated with transcriptional pausing and destabilization of forward translocation. This is complementary to the existing upstream GC-count split because it asks a more specific question about T enrichment in the last 8 nt rather than total GC across 10 nt, and it is distinct from the population because it does not use the already-popular downstream +2 region. The feature stays interpretable by using one contiguous short window and a simple count.
